en: Having bowed with speech, body, and mind to Mañjughoṣa, the teacher of the world, Aśvaghoṣa composes the *Vajrasūcī* according to his understanding.
The Vedas are authoritative; the Smṛtis are authoritative; speech endowed with righteousness and purpose is authoritative.
Who would accept as authoritative the word of one for whom authority itself is not authoritative?
The seven hunters were born among the Daśārṇas; the deer on Mount Kālañjara;
the cakravāka birds on Śaradvīpa; and the swans in Lake Mānasa.
They too were born in Kurukṣetra as Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas.
Having studied the four Vedas along with their limbs and sub-limbs,
a Brahmin who accepts gifts from a Śūdra is born as a donkey.
Manu has declared that such a person becomes a donkey for twelve births, a pig for sixty births, and a dog for seventy births.
Acala was born from Hastinī, Keśapiṅgala from Ulūkī;
Agastya arose from the Agasti flower, and Kauśika was produced from Kuśa grass.
Kapila was born from Kapilā, Gautama from Śaragulma;
Droṇācārya was born from a water-jar, and Tittiri was the son of Tittiri.
Reṇukā gave birth to Rāma, and the doe gave birth to the sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga;
Kaivartinī gave birth to Vyāsa, and Śūdrakā gave birth to Kuśika.
Viśvāmitra was born of a Caṇḍālī woman and Vasiṣṭha was born of Urvaśī;
yet, because of worldly custom, they are considered Brāhmaṇas, for their mothers were not Brāhmaṇa women.
One falls immediately from one's caste by selling meat, lac, or salt; and a Brāhmaṇa who sells milk becomes a Śūdra after three days.
Brahmins who travel through the sky fall because of eating meat;
seeing the downfall of brahmins, one should therefore avoid meats.
Therefore, the state of being a Brahmin does not arise through scripture, nor through consecratory rites, nor through castes;
it does not arise through lineage, nor through the Vedas, nor through ritual action.
Free from "mine-ness," free from egoism, unattached, and without possessions,
liberated from passion and hatred— the gods know him as a brāhmaṇa.
Truth is Brahman, austerity is Brahman, and the restraint of the senses is Brahman;
compassion toward all beings is Brahman—this is the defining characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa.
There is no truth, there is no austerity, there is no restraint of the senses,
and there is no compassion for all living beings— this is the characteristic of a Caṇḍāla.
They do not engage in sexual intercourse even with women of gods, humans, or those born of animal wombs; such are the wise ones, and they are the true Brāhmaṇas.
For birth is not what is seen; rather, it is virtues that bring about well-being.
Even if he is a caṇḍāla, the gods recognize him as a brahmin if he abides therein.
For one who has drunk the saliva of a low-caste woman, who has been defiled by her breath,
and who has procreated with her, no atonement is found.
He who eats continuously for one month with the hand of a Śūdra woman shall become a Śūdra while alive and, upon death, is born as a dog.
A Brahmin surrounded by a Śūdra woman, with a Śūdra woman as his housewife,
being abandoned by the ancestors and the gods, goes to the Raurava hell.
The great sage named Kaṭha was born from within the fire-drill (araṇī);
he became a Brāhmaṇa through asceticism (tapas). Therefore, birth is not the cause [of one's status].
The great sage named Vyāsa was born from the womb of a fisherwoman;
he became a Brāhmaṇa through ascetic penance. Therefore, birth is not the cause [of one's status].
Even the great sage Vasiṣṭha, though born from the womb of Urvaśī, became a Brāhmaṇa through asceticism; therefore, birth is not the cause [of being a Brāhmaṇa].
The great sage Ṛṣyaśṛṅga was born from the womb of a deer;
he became a Brāhmaṇa through asceticism. Therefore, birth is not the cause [of one's status].
The great sage Viśvāmitra was born from the womb of a Caṇḍālī;
he became a Brāhmaṇa through asceticism. Therefore, birth is not the cause [of one's status].
For the great sage Nārada was born from the womb of a grain of rice;
he became a Brahmin through asceticism. Therefore, birth is not the cause [of being a Brahmin].
One who has conquered the self becomes an ascetic... one who has conquered the senses;
[one whose self is restrained becomes an ascetic—one who has conquered the self and conquered the senses.]
Through austerity one becomes an ascetic; through celibacy one becomes a Brahmin.
And those sons of a Brāhmaṇī are not [true] Brāhmaṇas in the eyes of the world;
Brahman consists of virtue and purity, therefore lineage is not the cause.
Virtue is primary, not noble birth; for what is the use of birth in a high family if it is devoid of virtue?
Many wise men born of lowly families have gone to heaven by resorting to virtue.
The Brāhmaṇa was born from the mouth, and likewise the Kṣatriya from the two arms;
the Vaiśya was born from the two thighs, and the Śūdra indeed from the two feet.
The renowned son of Pāṇḍu, indeed named Yudhiṣṭhira,
approached Vaiśampāyana and, with palms joined in reverence, questioned him.
Who are those called brahmins, and what is the defining characteristic of a brahmin? O sir, I wish to know this; may you explain it to me.
Endowed with virtues such as patience, having laid aside the rod and being free from worldly desire, one does not harm any living beings; this is the first characteristic of a Brahmin.
When one never takes anything that has not been given— whether it be another's property on the road or in the house— this is the second characteristic of a Brahmin.
Having abandoned his cruel nature, free from the sense of "mine" and without possessions,
he who wanders eternally liberated [exhibits] the third characteristic of a Brahmin.
Sexual intercourse has indeed been forever abandoned by women among gods and humans, as well as even those born of animal wombs; this is the fourth characteristic of a Brahmin.
Truthfulness is purity, cleanliness is purity, restraint of the senses is purity;
compassion toward all beings is purity, and austerity is the fifth purity.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I would call that twice-born man a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with these five characteristics; all others are Śūdras.
One does not become a brahmin by lineage or by birth, nor by ritual acts;
for even a caṇḍāla who abides in right conduct, O Yudhiṣṭhira, is a brahmin.
Non-violence, celibacy, and pure acceptance of gifts—
O Yudhiṣṭhira, a Brāhmaṇa should not be capable of these for the sake of fruit.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this entire universe was formerly of a single caste;
it was through the distinction of actions and rituals that the fourfold caste system became established.
All mortals are indeed born from a womb; all possess urine and excrement;
and all have sense organs and objects of the senses. Therefore, O twice-born ones, [one is distinguished] by the qualities of virtuous conduct.
Even a Śūdra who is endowed with virtuous conduct and possesses good qualities may become a Brāhmaṇa;
whereas even a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of ritual action is inferior to a Śūdra.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, if even a Śūdra has crossed the terrible ocean of the five senses,
one should bestow immeasurable gifts upon him.

O King, birth is not seen [as the defining factor]; rather, virtues are what bring about well-being. Those whose life is for the sake of Dharma, and whose life is for the sake of others—those who practice patience day and night, the gods know them as Brahmins.
O son of Kuntī, O Yudhiṣṭhira, those who have abandoned the life of a householder and remain intent on seeking liberation, being unattached to sensual pleasures, are Brāhmaṇas.
Non-violence, freedom from possessiveness, the avoidance of what is not one's duty, and the cessation of passion and hatred— this is the defining characteristic of a Brahmin.
Forbearance, compassion, self-restraint, generosity, truthfulness, purity, mindfulness, mercy, learning, discernment, and faith— this is the characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa.
A Brahmin who is well-restrained is better, even if his essence consists only of the Gāyatrī,
than one who is unrestrained, though he may know the four Vedas, eat all things, and sell all things.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, that destination which belongs even to a celibate student who has stayed for only a single night cannot be attained by means of a thousand sacrifices.
They know him alone to be a Brāhmaṇa who has reached the further shore of all Vedas, who has performed ablutions at all sacred fords, and who lives as one liberated while practicing the Dharma.
When one commits no cruel evil toward any living being by means of body, mind, or speech, then one attains Brahman.
"We have spoken this in order to destroy the delusion of these twice-born ones whose intellects are ruined;
let the virtuous accept it if it is reasonable, or reject it if it should be unreasonable. (Vs 53)
This work is the composition of the feet of the accomplished master Aśvaghoṣa; thus ends the *Vajrasūcī*. May there be auspiciousness!
